Sergio, it is Marina. Ten minutes on Tuesday, and there are three things I want in your head before you stand up. First, write eight minutes of material, not ten. Everybody speaks slower standing up than they do at a rehearsal, and the room forgives a thin minute at the end. What it does not forgive is overrunning, because the four minutes you take are not yours; they come out of whoever is speaking after you, and that person will remember it. Second, and this is the one that changes how the ten minutes sound. Decide, before you write anything, which three sentences you want them to repeat to somebody else afterwards. Three. Build those three so that the important part lands at the end, and say everything else flat, on purpose. If you put weight on the fourth one, it cancels the first three, and the room stops hearing any of them. Third, the last sentence. Write your closing remark before you write the nine minutes in front of it, because that is the sentence they carry out of the room. And never end with that is it, or with any questions. End with the thing you are asking them to approve, said in full, and then be quiet and let them answer.

Sergio, Paulo here, from the credit desk. Two things about how it actually goes in that room, and neither is about grammar. The first one is the pause. When you need two seconds to find the next idea, you have a choice: make a small empty sound, or say nothing. It is the same two seconds either way, but a filler sounds like a man looking for a word, and silence sounds like a man who has decided something. Nobody has ever thought less of a presenter for pausing. The second one is the interruption, and this is where most people lose the ten minutes. Somebody will cut in halfway through with a question about the model. Do not follow them. Answer in one line, say out loud that you are coming back to it, finish the point you were on, and then circle back. If you abandon the line you were on, you will not find it again with eight people watching you. And an aside is fine, but say that it is one and close it in a sentence. If you digress without telling anybody, the room walks off the plan with you, and when you come back nobody can tell which part was the plan and which part was the story.

First, open with what the room has to decide today, and put the decision at the end of the sentence. Then walk through the lines of the plan with one date next to each of them. Next, correct the one thing the room has wrong, picking that part out with it was and that. After that, take the interruption in one line, finish the point you were on, and circle back. Finally, land on the closing remark you wrote before the rest, and then stop talking.
What this committee needs is one number on one page.
What the plan needs is two more weeks of lead time.
